title: Ἡ χλαῖνα καὶ ὁ ὅρκος
titleEn: The Cloak, the Brooch and the Oath — Odyssey 19.203–307
part: The Cloak, the Brooch and the Oath (19.203–307)
source: Homer, The Odyssey, Greek text of A. T. Murray (Loeb Classical Library; London: Heinemann, New York: Putnam, 1919), public domain; TEI from PerseusDL/canonical-greekLit tlg0012.tlg002.perseus-grc2, sha256 7d7ffafb6c51f8c2. Text as printed: Murray sets no quotation marks round speeches, and none are added. Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca — an admitted convention; Homer's own pronunciation was older and is not recoverable in detail. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; ï for a separately sounded ι; accents omitted). Scansion: made by program from the text and checked; it shows one defensible reading of each line, and the notes say where a line is irregular. All translations were made fresh from the Greek for Lectorium.
about: The stranger’s tale of Crete takes Penelope to tears, and she weeps like snow melting into rivers, while Odysseus, pitying her, keeps his eyes still as horn or iron and hides his own tears by craft. When she has wept her fill she says she will now test him: if he really entertained her husband, let him describe the clothes Odysseus wore and the companions who followed him. He describes a double purple cloak with a golden brooch, a hound gripping a struggling fawn, a tunic as glossy as onion-skin, and a herald named Eurybates, round-shouldered, dark-skinned and woolly-haired. Penelope knows the signs for true, since she herself gave him the clothes and the brooch, and she promises the stranger a warm welcome; but she says that Odysseus is gone for good to Evil-Ilium. Odysseus bids her stop mourning and tells her what he heard in Thesprotia: Odysseus is alive, gathering treasure, and has gone to Dodona to learn how to come home; he will be home this very year, and the stranger swears to it by Zeus and by the hearth of Odysseus.

sentences.t: ἴσκε ψεύδεα πολλὰ λέγων ἐτύμοισιν ὁμοῖα·
sentences.tr: iske pseudea polla legōn etymoisin homoia·
sentences.l: He made-like, telling many lies, to true things resembling;
sentences.i: He told many lies, and gave them the likeness of true things;
sentences.n: ἴσκε is the imperfect of ἴσκω ‘make like, represent as’, here with ψεύδεα ‘lies’ as its object and ἐτύμοισιν ὁμοῖα ‘like to true things’ completing it; λέγων ‘in the telling’ is the manner. ἐτύμοισιν is a dative plural in -οισιν. The line looks back on the Cretan tale of the last part, and this unit runs on from it without a speech: it is narration.

sentences.t: τῆς δ’ ἄρ’ ἀκουούσης ῥέε δάκρυα, τήκετο δὲ χρώς·
sentences.tr: tēs d’ ar’ akouousēs rhee dakrya, tēketo de chrōs·
sentences.l: And as she listened, tears flowed, and her skin melted;
sentences.i: And as she listened, her tears flowed and her skin melted away;
sentences.n: τῆς ἀκουούσης is a genitive absolute, ‘she listening’ (τῆς is the pronoun ‘she’); ῥέε is the uncontracted imperfect of ῥέω ‘flow’, and δάκρυα is ‘tears’. χρώς is ‘skin’, the body’s surface. τήκετο, the imperfect middle of τήκω ‘melt’, is the word on which the next lines build their image.

sentences.t:
ὡς δὲ χιὼν κατατήκετ’ ἐν ἀκροπόλοισιν ὄρεσσιν,
ἥν τ’ Εὖρος κατέτηξεν, ἐπὴν Ζέφυρος καταχεύῃ·
sentences.tr:
hōs de chiōn katatēket’ en akropoloisin oressin,
hēn t’ Euros katetēxen, epēn Zephyros katacheuēi·
sentences.l:
And as snow melts away on the high mountains,
which the East Wind has melted, when the West Wind has poured it down;
sentences.i: As snow melts away on the high mountains, snow that the East Wind has thawed once the West Wind has poured it down;
sentences.n: ὡς δέ … ὣς (208) is a simile: ‘as … so’. κατατήκετ’ is κατατήκεται with elision, ‘melts away’. ἀκροπόλοισιν is a dative plural in -οισιν of the adjective ἀκρόπολος ‘on the heights’, and ὄρεσσιν is the epic dative plural of ὄρος ‘mountain’. ἥν is the relative, ‘which’ (the snow), and τε is the epic particle of a general statement. Εὖρος and Ζέφυρος are two winds, here ‘the East Wind’ and ‘the West Wind’; κατέτηξεν is the aorist of κατατήκω ‘melt’ (transitive here), and καταχεύῃ is an aorist subjunctive of καταχέω ‘pour down’, after ἐπήν ‘when’ (ἐπεί with ἄν fused into it). The sense is that the West Wind lays the snow down and the East Wind thaws it.

sentences.t: τηκομένης δ’ ἄρα τῆς ποταμοὶ πλήθουσι ῥέοντες·
sentences.tr: tēkomenēs d’ ara tēs potamoi plēthousi rheontes·
sentences.l: and as it melts, the rivers fill, flowing;
sentences.i: and as it melts, the rivers fill as they flow;
sentences.n: τηκομένης … τῆς is another genitive absolute, ‘it (the snow) melting’; τῆς is the pronoun again. πλήθουσι is the present of πλήθω ‘be full’, and ῥέοντες is the participle ‘flowing’, uncontracted. The rivers filling is the picture of the flooding tears.

sentences.t:
ὣς τῆς τήκετο καλὰ παρήϊα δάκρυ χεούσης,
κλαιούσης ἑὸν ἄνδρα παρήμενον.
sentences.tr:
hōs tēs tēketo kala parēïa dakry cheousēs,
klaiousēs heon andra parēmenon.
sentences.l:
so her fair cheeks melted as she shed a tear,
weeping for her own husband, who sat beside her.
sentences.i: so her fair cheeks melted as she shed her tears, weeping for her own husband, who sat beside her.
sentences.n: ὣς … τήκετο completes the simile: ‘so her cheeks melted’. τῆς … χεούσης and κλαιούσης are genitive participles agreeing with τῆς, ‘she shedding, she weeping’ (the stock phrase δάκρυ χέων ‘shedding a tear’ is here feminine). παρήϊα is ‘cheeks’, the neuter plural of παρήϊον, with the uncontracted epic ending. ἑόν is the possessive ‘her own’, from ἑός, not the relative; and παρήμενον is the participle ‘sitting beside’. The husband sits beside her without her knowing it: the irony of the scene. The unit ends with a full stop inside line 209.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ Ὀδυσσεὺς
θυμῷ μὲν γοόωσαν ἑὴν ἐλέαιρε γυναῖκα,
ὀφθαλμοὶ δ’ ὡς εἰ κέρα ἕστασαν ἠὲ σίδηρος
ἀτρέμας ἐν βλεφάροισι·
sentences.tr:
autar Odysseus
thymōi men gooōsan heēn eleaire gynaika,
ophthalmoi d’ hōs ei kera hestasan ēe sidēros
atremas en blepharoisi·
sentences.l:
But Odysseus
in his heart pitied his own wife as she lamented,
and his eyes, as if horn or iron, stood
unmoving in his eyelids;
sentences.i: But Odysseus pitied his own wife in his heart as she lamented, while his eyes stood unmoving in their lids as though they were horn or iron;
sentences.n: αὐτάρ ‘but’ opens the contrast. θυμῷ is ‘in his heart’ (dative of place), and γοόωσαν is the uncontracted participle of γοάω ‘lament’, with ἑήν ‘his own’ the possessive again. ὀφθαλμοὶ … ἕστασαν is the pluperfect of ἵστημι, ‘stood’, and κέρα (the epic neuter plural of κέρας) is ‘horn’, the material; ὡς εἰ is ‘as if’. ἀτρέμας is the adverb ‘unmoving, without a tremor’, and βλεφάροισι is a dative plural in -οισι ‘in the eyelids’. His body is as hard as his feelings are soft.

sentences.t: δόλῳ δ’ ὅ γε δάκρυα κεῦθεν.
sentences.tr: dolōi d’ ho ge dakrya keuthen.
sentences.l: and by guile he, for his part, hid the tears.
sentences.i: and by guile he kept his tears hidden.
sentences.n: δόλῳ is a dative of means, ‘by craft’; ὅ γε is ‘he’ (pronoun), and κεῦθεν is the imperfect of κεύθω ‘hide, keep hidden’, with no augment. The point of the line is that Odysseus is the stranger and Penelope does not know it.

sentences.t:
ἡ δ’ ἐπεὶ οὖν τάρφθη πολυδακρύτοιο γόοιο,
ἐξαῦτίς μιν ἔπεσσιν ἀμειβομένη προσέειπε·
sentences.tr:
hē d’ epei oun tarphthē polydakrytoio gooio,
exautis min epessin ameibomenē proseeipe·
sentences.l:
And she, when she had had her fill of much-wept lament,
again with words, answering, addressed him:
sentences.i: And when she had had her fill of lament and many tears, she answered him again, and spoke:
sentences.n: ἡ is ‘she’ (pronoun), and τάρφθη is the aorist passive of τέρπω ‘delight’, here ‘had her fill’, taking the genitive γόοιο ‘lament’; πολυδακρύτοιο (genitive in -οιο) is built on δάκρυ and means ‘much-wept’, ‘of many tears’. ἐξαῦτις is ‘again, once more’. The reply-formula μιν ἔπεσσιν ἀμειβομένη προσέειπε is ‘answering him with words she addressed him’; ἔπεσσιν is a dative plural in -εσσι(ν), and προσέειπε is the aorist of προσεῖπον, with the Homeric double ε.

sentences.t:
νῦν μὲν δή σευ, ξεῖνέ γ’, ὀΐω πειρήσεσθαι,
εἰ ἐτεὸν δὴ κεῖθι σὺν ἀντιθέοις ἑτάροισι
ξείνισας ἐν μεγάροισιν ἐμὸν πόσιν, ὡς ἀγορεύεις.
sentences.tr:
nyn men dē seu, xeine g’, oïō peirēsesthai,
ei eteon dē keithi syn antitheois hetaroisi
xeinisas en megaroisin emon posin, hōs agoreueis.
sentences.l:
“Now indeed of you, stranger, I think I shall make trial,
whether in truth there, along with godlike companions,
you entertained in your halls my husband, as you say.
sentences.i: “Now, stranger, I think I shall try you, to learn whether you truly entertained my husband there in your halls, together with his godlike companions, as you say.
sentences.n: Penelope turns the tale into a test. νῦν μὲν δή is ‘now indeed’, and σευ is the epic genitive of σύ, governed by πειρήσεσθαι ‘to make trial of’ (the future infinitive middle, after ὀΐω ‘I think’). εἰ ἐτεὸν δή is ‘whether in truth’, κεῖθι ‘there’ (the suffix -θι marks place), and ἀντιθέοις ἑτάροισι are ‘godlike companions’, in datives in -οις and -οισι; they are Odysseus’s men, as lines 218–219 show. ξείνισας is the aorist of ξεινίζω ‘entertain as a guest’, and ἐμὸν πόσιν is ‘my husband’.

sentences.t:
εἰπέ μοι ὁπποῖ’ ἄσσα περὶ χροῒ εἵματα ἕστο,
αὐτός θ’ οἷος ἔην, καὶ ἑταίρους, οἵ οἱ ἕποντο.
sentences.tr:
eipe moi hoppoi’ assa peri chroï heimata hesto,
autos th’ hoios eēn, kai hetairous, hoi hoi heponto.
sentences.l:
Tell me what sort of clothes he wore about his skin,
and what kind of man he himself was, and the companions who followed him.”
sentences.i: Tell me what clothes he wore on his body, what he himself was like, and who the companions were that followed him.”
sentences.n: εἰπέ is the aorist imperative of λέγω, and ὁπποῖ’ ἄσσα is ὁποῖα ἅττα ‘what sort of things’ with the neuter plural elided; ἕστο is the pluperfect middle of ἕννυμι, ‘he had on, was clothed in’, with χροῒ ‘on his skin’. αὐτός θ’ οἷος ἔην is ‘and what sort he himself was’ (ἔην is ‘was’, epic for ἦν), and ἑταίρους is a second object of εἰπέ. The companions that followed (ἕποντο, imperfect of ἕπομαι) are the second part of the test: a liar could not easily invent them all.

sentences.t: τὴν δ’ ἀπαμειβόμενος προσέφη πολύμητις Ὀδυσσεύς·
sentences.tr: tēn d’ apameibomenos prosephē polymētis Odysseus·
sentences.l: Her answering addressed many-wiled Odysseus:
sentences.i: In answer Odysseus of many wiles said to her:
sentences.n: τὴν δ’ ἀπαμειβόμενος προσέφη is the reply-formula: τήν is ‘her’ (the article as pronoun), ἀπαμειβόμενος ‘answering’, and προσέφη is the aorist ‘addressed’. πολύμητις ‘of many wiles’ is the stock epithet of Odysseus, translated the same way each time; it is built on μῆτις ‘cunning intelligence’. The words introduce the stranger’s answer, which begins in the next unit.

sentences.t:
ὦ γύναι, ἀργαλέον τόσσον χρόνον ἀμφὶς ἐόντα
εἰπέμεν·
sentences.tr:
ō gynai, argaleon tosson chronon amphis eonta
eipemen·
sentences.l:
“O woman, it is grievous, one so long a time apart,
to tell;
sentences.i: “Woman, it is grievous for one so long apart to tell it;
sentences.n: ὦ γύναι is ‘O woman’, the plain unmarked address. ἀργαλέον ‘grievous, hard’ takes the infinitive εἰπέμεν, the epic infinitive in -έμεν (Attic εἰπεῖν), and the accusative ἐόντα (ἐών, ‘being’) agrees with an unexpressed ‘me’: ‘it is grievous for one being so long apart to tell’. ἀμφίς is ‘apart’, and τόσσον χρόνον is ‘so long a time’ (accusative of duration). He gives himself an excuse for what comes next: a man remembers badly after twenty years.

sentences.t:
ἤδη γάρ οἱ ἐεικοστὸν ἔτος ἐστὶν
ἐξ οὗ κεῖθεν ἔβη καὶ ἐμῆς ἀπελήλυθε πάτρης·
sentences.tr:
ēdē gar hoi eeikoston etos estin
ex hou keithen ebē kai emēs apelēlythe patrēs·
sentences.l:
for already to him a twentieth year it is
since he went from there and departed from my fatherland;
sentences.i: for it is already the twentieth year since he went away from there and left my fatherland;
sentences.n: οἱ is ‘to him’ (a dative of interest), and ἐεικοστὸν ἔτος is ‘a twentieth year’, ἐεικοστός being the epic form (Attic εἰκοστός). ἐξ οὗ is ‘since’, κεῖθεν ‘from there’ (-θεν marks the point of departure), and ἔβη is the aorist of βαίνω ‘go’; ἀπελήλυθε is the perfect of ἀπέρχομαι ‘has gone away’. ἐμῆς … πάτρης is ‘my fatherland’, Crete in the tale, and πάτρη is the Ionic noun beside πατρίς. Twenty years is the true length of Odysseus’s absence, and Penelope hears it as such.

sentences.t: αὐτάρ τοι ἐρέω ὥς μοι ἰνδάλλεται ἦτορ.
sentences.tr: autar toi ereō hōs moi indalletai ētor.
sentences.l: but I will tell you as my heart shows it to me.
sentences.i: but I will tell you as my heart presents it to me.
sentences.n: αὐτάρ ‘but’, τοι is the epic ‘to you’ (σοι), and ἐρέω is the future of εἶπον ‘I will say’. ὥς … ἰνδάλλεται is ‘as my heart shows it to me’: ἰνδάλλομαι is ‘show oneself, appear’, with ἦτορ ‘heart’ most simply as its subject (it could also be an accusative of respect, ‘in my heart’) and μοι ‘to me’. The meaning of the verb is not certain beyond ‘appear, seem’; the English follows that sense. A promise of honesty from a man who is lying about his identity.

sentences.t:
χλαῖναν πορφυρέην οὔλην ἔχε δῖος Ὀδυσσεύς,
διπλῆν·
sentences.tr:
chlainan porphyreēn oulēn eche dios Odysseus,
diplēn·
sentences.l:
A purple cloak, thick, wore heavenly Odysseus,
double;
sentences.i: Heavenly Odysseus wore a thick purple cloak, a double one;
sentences.n: χλαῖναν πορφυρέην is ‘a purple cloak’ (πορφυρέη ‘purple’); ἔχε is the imperfect ‘was wearing’. οὔλην is the accusative of οὖλος, ‘thick’ (it can also mean ‘woolly’; the house word for a cloak is ‘thick’), so a heavy wool cloak, and διπλῆν ‘double’ is the cloak folded in two. δῖος Ὀδυσσεύς is ‘heavenly Odysseus’ by the house rendering of δῖος (not ‘divine’, which stands for θεῖος). The word-order puts the object first, before the verb.

sentences.t:
αὐτάρ οἱ περόνη χρυσοῖο τέτυκτο
αὐλοῖσιν διδύμοισι· πάροιθε δὲ δαίδαλον ἦεν·
sentences.tr:
autar hoi peronē chrysoio tetykto
auloisin didymoisi· paroithe de daidalon ēen·
sentences.l:
and for him a brooch of gold had been made
with twin pipes; and in front it was cunningly wrought;
sentences.i: and he had a brooch of gold, made with twin tubes; and in front it was cunningly wrought;
sentences.n: The brooch (περόνη) is the pin that fastens the cloak; οἱ is ‘for him’, and τέτυκτο is the pluperfect passive of τεύχω ‘had been made’, with χρυσοῖο ‘of gold’ as a genitive in -οιο. αὐλοῖσιν διδύμοισι is ‘with twin pipes’: αὐλός is ‘pipe, tube’, here the tubes or sheaths of the brooch, though how they worked is not clear, and the dative is a dative of means. πάροιθε is ‘in front’, and δαίδαλον ἦεν is ‘was cunningly wrought’ (ἦεν is ἦν ‘was’).

sentences.t:
ἐν προτέροισι πόδεσσι κύων ἔχε ποικίλον ἐλλόν,
ἀσπαίροντα λάων·
sentences.tr:
en proteroisi podessi kyōn eche poikilon ellon,
aspaironta laōn·
sentences.l:
In its forefeet a hound held a dappled fawn,
struggling, gripping it;
sentences.i: A hound held a dappled fawn in its forefeet and gripped it as it struggled;
sentences.n: The design on the brooch begins. προτέροισι πόδεσσι are ‘forefeet’ (datives in -οισι and -εσσι), κύων is ‘hound’, and ποικίλον ἐλλόν is ‘a dappled fawn’ (ἐλλός is ‘fawn’, ποικίλος ‘dappled’ here, of a pattern of spots). ἀσπαίροντα is the present participle of ἀσπαίρω ‘struggle, gasp’. λάων is a participle of λάω, whose meaning is not known: the ancient guesses are ‘gaze at’ and ‘grip, seize’, and the English takes ‘grip’ as the guess.

sentences.t:
τὸ δὲ θαυμάζεσκον ἅπαντες,
ὡς οἱ χρύσεοι ἐόντες ὁ μὲν λάε νεβρὸν ἀπάγχων,
αὐτὰρ ὁ ἐκφυγέειν μεμαὼς ἤσπαιρε πόδεσσι.
sentences.tr:
to de thaumazeskon hapantes,
hōs hoi chryseoi eontes ho men lae nebron apanchōn,
autar ho ekphygeein memaōs ēspaire podessi.
sentences.l:
and at it all marvelled,
how, golden as they were, the one gripped the fawn, throttling it,
but the other, eager to escape, struggled with his feet.
sentences.i: and all marvelled at it, how, golden though they were, the one gripped the fawn, throttling it, while the other, eager to escape, struggled with his feet.
sentences.n: τό is ‘it’, the brooch, and θαυμάζεσκον is an iterative imperfect in -σκον ‘used to marvel’, ‘all marvelled’. ὡς is ‘how’. οἱ here is best taken as the pronoun ‘they’, anticipating ὁ μέν … ὁ δέ ‘the one … the other’: the golden hound and the golden fawn; χρύσεοι ἐόντες is ‘being of gold’. λάε is the imperfect of λάω (see the previous unit for the doubtful meaning) with ἀπάγχων ‘throttling’. ἐκφυγέειν is an aorist infinitive in -έειν, ‘to escape’, with μεμαώς ‘eager’ (perfect participle of μέμονα), and ἤσπαιρε is the imperfect of ἀσπαίρω, ‘struggled’, with πόδεσσι ‘with its feet’.

sentences.t:
τὸν δὲ χιτῶν’ ἐνόησα περὶ χροῒ σιγαλόεντα,
οἷόν τε κρομύοιο λοπὸν κάτα ἰσχαλέοιο·
sentences.tr:
ton de chitōn’ enoēsa peri chroï sigaloenta,
hoion te kromyoio lopon kata ischaleoio·
sentences.l:
And the tunic I perceived about his skin, glossy,
such as is, along the skin of a dried onion;
sentences.i: And the tunic I saw about his body was glossy, like the skin of a dried onion;
sentences.n: τὸν δὲ χιτῶν’ ἐνόησα is ‘and that tunic I noticed’: τόν is ‘that’, χιτῶν’ is the accusative with elision of -α, and ἐνόησα the aorist ‘noticed’. σιγαλόεντα is ‘glossy’, as of fine cloth. οἷόν τε is ‘such as is’ (the sense is ‘like’), and λοπὸν κάτα is ‘along the skin’ (λοπός ‘peel, skin’, accusative after κάτα) of an onion (κρομύοιο, genitive in -οιο) that is ἰσχαλέοιο ‘dried’; κάτα is κατά placed after its noun (anastrophe). The exact force of κάτα is not clear, but the sense is a thin, glossy, dry-looking skin.

sentences.t: τὼς μὲν ἔην μαλακός, λαμπρὸς δ’ ἦν ἠέλιος ὥς·
sentences.tr: tōs men eēn malakos, lampros d’ ēn ēelios hōs·
sentences.l: so soft it was, and bright as the sun;
sentences.i: so soft it was, and it shone like the sun;
sentences.n: τώς is ‘so’ (Attic οὕτως), and ἔην is ‘was’, μαλακός ‘soft’. λαμπρός δ’ ἦν is ‘and it was bright’, and ἠέλιος ὥς is ‘like the sun’, with ὥς following the noun: ἠέλιος is the epic form of ἥλιος.

sentences.t: ἦ μὲν πολλαί γ’ αὐτὸν ἐθηήσαντο γυναῖκες.
sentences.tr: ē men pollai g’ auton ethēēsanto gynaikes.
sentences.l: Truly many women gazed at it in wonder.
sentences.i: Indeed, many women gazed at it in admiration.
sentences.n: ἦ μέν is ‘truly’, and αὐτόν is ‘it’ (the tunic is masculine, χιτών). ἐθηήσαντο is the aorist middle of θηέομαι ‘gaze at, admire’, in the uncontracted epic form (Attic θεάομαι). The women are not identified.

sentences.t: ἄλλο δέ τοι ἐρέω, σὺ δ’ ἐνὶ φρεσὶ βάλλεο σῇσιν·
sentences.tr: allo de toi ereō, sy d’ eni phresi balleo sēisin·
sentences.l: And another thing to you I will say, and you in your own mind lay it:
sentences.i: And I will tell you something else; lay it up in your own mind:
sentences.n: ἄλλο δέ τοι ἐρέω is ‘and another thing I will tell you’, with τοι the epic ‘to you’ and ἐρέω the future of εἶπον. σὺ δ’ ἐνὶ φρεσὶ βάλλεο σῇσιν is ‘and lay it in your own mind’: βάλλεο is the imperative middle ‘put, lay’ with the uncontracted ending -εο, and σῇσιν is a dative plural in -ῃσι, ‘in your own wits’.

sentences.t:
οὐκ οἶδ’ ἢ τάδε ἕστο περὶ χροῒ οἴκοθ’ Ὀδυσσεύς,
ἦ τις ἑταίρων δῶκε θοῆς ἐπὶ νηὸς ἰόντι,
ἤ τίς που καὶ ξεῖνος, ἐπεὶ πολλοῖσιν Ὀδυσσεὺς
ἔσκε φίλος·
sentences.tr:
ouk oid’ ē tade hesto peri chroï oikoth’ Odysseus,
ē tis hetairōn dōke thoēs epi nēos ionti,
ē tis pou kai xeinos, epei polloisin Odysseus
eske philos·
sentences.l:
I do not know whether Odysseus wore these things about his skin from home,
or some one of his companions gave them to him, going upon the swift ship,
or perhaps even some guest-friend, since to many Odysseus
was dear;
sentences.i: I do not know whether Odysseus wore these things on his body when he left home, or one of his companions gave them to him as he boarded the swift ship, or perhaps even some guest-friend; for to many Odysseus was dear;
sentences.n: οὐκ οἶδ’ ἢ … ἦ … ἤ is ‘I do not know whether … or … or’. τάδε ἕστο is ‘wore these things’ (ἕστο, pluperfect middle of ἕννυμι), and οἴκοθ’ is οἴκοθεν ‘from home’ with the ending -θεν elided. δῶκε is the unaugmented aorist ‘gave’, with the dative participle ἰόντι ‘to him going’ (εἶμι), and θοῆς ἐπὶ νηός is ‘on the swift ship’ (νηῦς θοή). ξεῖνος here is the ‘guest-friend’, someone bound to him by the guest-bond. ἔσκε is the iterative of εἰμί, ‘was’, and φίλος is ‘dear’. The cloak’s origin is left open on purpose, since that is how he keeps from claiming too much.

sentences.t: παῦροι γὰρ Ἀχαιῶν ἦσαν ὁμοῖοι.
sentences.tr: pauroi gar Achaiōn ēsan homoioi.
sentences.l: for few of the Achaeans were his like.
sentences.i: for few of the Achaeans were his equals.
sentences.n: παῦροι is ‘few’, and Ἀχαιῶν is a partitive genitive ‘of the Achaeans’; ἦσαν ὁμοῖοι is ‘were like’, with the person unexpressed (‘like him’). The reason (γάρ) is for the many guest-friends of the previous unit.

sentences.t:
καί οἱ ἐγὼ χάλκειον ἄορ καὶ δίπλακα δῶκα
καλὴν πορφυρέην καὶ τερμιόεντα χιτῶνα,
αἰδοίως δ’ ἀπέπεμπον ἐϋσσέλμου ἐπὶ νηός.
sentences.tr:
kai hoi egō chalkeion aor kai diplaka dōka
kalēn porphyreēn kai termioenta chitōna,
aidoiōs d’ apepempon eÿsselmou epi nēos.
sentences.l:
and to him I gave a bronze sword and a double cloak,
fair, purple, and a tunic with a border,
and with respect I sent him off to the well-benched ship.
sentences.i: I gave him a bronze sword and a fair purple double cloak, and a bordered tunic, and with respect I sent him off to his well-benched ship.
sentences.n: Now the stranger says he gave Odysseus gifts. χάλκειον ἄορ is ‘a bronze sword’, and δίπλακα is the accusative of δίπλαξ ‘a double cloak’, which the adjectives καλήν and πορφυρέην ‘fair, purple’ agree with. τερμιόεντα is of an uncertain sense: from τέρμα ‘end, limit’, so probably ‘with a border’. δῶκα is the aorist ‘I gave’, αἰδοίως ‘with respect’ is the adverb of αἰδοῖος, and ἀπέπεμπον is the imperfect ‘I was sending off’. ἐϋσσέλμου … νηός is ‘of the well-benched ship’ (ἐύσσελμος, the stock epithet of a ship), with ἐπί and the genitive meaning ‘to’ the ship.

sentences.t:
καὶ μέν οἱ κῆρυξ ὀλίγον προγενέστερος αὐτοῦ
εἵπετο·
sentences.tr:
kai men hoi kēryx oligon progenesteros autou
heipeto·
sentences.l:
And indeed a herald, a little older than he,
was following him;
sentences.i: A herald, a little older than he was, went with him;
sentences.n: καὶ μέν is ‘and indeed’. κῆρυξ is ‘herald’, and ὀλίγον is the adverbial accusative ‘a little’, with προγενέστερος ‘born earlier, older’ and the genitive αὐτοῦ of comparison, ‘than himself’. οἱ is ‘him’ (dative with εἵπετο), and εἵπετο is the imperfect of ἕπομαι ‘follow’. The herald answers the last of Penelope’s requests (lines 218–219).

sentences.t: καὶ τόν τοι μυθήσομαι, οἷος ἔην περ.
sentences.tr: kai ton toi mythēsomai, hoios eēn per.
sentences.l: and him too I will describe to you, just as he was.
sentences.i: I will describe him to you as well, just as he was.
sentences.n: τόν is ‘him’, the herald, and τοι is ‘to you’. μυθήσομαι is the future of μυθέομαι ‘tell, speak of’, and οἷος ἔην περ is ‘just what sort he was’, with περ ‘just’ sharpening οἷος. The unit begins after the raised dot in line 245 and ends at the full stop that closes the line.

sentences.t:
γυρὸς ἐν ὤμοισιν, μελανόχροος, οὐλοκάρηνος,
Εὐρυβάτης δ’ ὄνομ’ ἔσκε·
sentences.tr:
gyros en ōmoisin, melanochroos, oulokarēnos,
Eurybatēs d’ onom’ eske·
sentences.l:
rounded in the shoulders, dark-skinned, woolly-headed,
and Eurybates his name was;
sentences.i: He was round-shouldered, dark-skinned and woolly-haired, and his name was Eurybates;
sentences.n: γυρός is ‘curved’, so ‘round-shouldered’, with ἐν ὤμοισιν ‘in the shoulders’. μελανόχροος ‘dark-skinned’ is μέλας ‘black’ with χρώς ‘skin’ (see line 204), and οὐλοκάρηνος is ‘woolly-headed’, οὖλος ‘woolly’ with κάρη ‘head’. Εὐρυβάτης is Eurybates, a man’s name. ὄνομ’ ἔσκε is ‘name was’, ἔσκε being the iterative of εἰμί. The three adjectives are asyndeton: no ‘and’, only commas.

sentences.t:
τίεν δέ μιν ἔξοχον ἄλλων
ὧν ἑτάρων Ὀδυσεύς, ὅτι οἱ φρεσὶν ἄρτια ᾔδη.
sentences.tr:
tien de min exochon allōn
hōn hetarōn Odyseus, hoti hoi phresin artia ēidē.
sentences.l:
and Odysseus honored him above others
of his own companions, because his mind was fitted to his own.”
sentences.i: and Odysseus honored him above the rest of his companions, because his mind was fitted to his own.”
sentences.n: τίεν is the unaugmented imperfect of τίω ‘honor’. μιν is ‘him’, ἔξοχον ἄλλων is ‘above others’, and ὧν ἑτάρων is ‘of his own companions’ with ὧν the possessive (not a relative). ὅτι οἱ φρεσὶν ἄρτια ᾔδη is ‘because in his mind he knew fitting things’: ἄρτια is ‘fitting’, ᾔδη the pluperfect of οἶδα with the sense of an imperfect; the English takes it as an idiom for being of one mind with Odysseus, though the grammar of οἱ does not itself settle whose mind is meant. The speech ends here.

sentences.t:
ὣς φάτο, τῇ δ’ ἔτι μᾶλλον ὑφ’ ἵμερον ὦρσε γόοιο,
σήματ’ ἀναγνούσῃ τά οἱ ἔμπεδα πέφραδ’ Ὀδυσσεύς.
sentences.tr:
hōs phato, tēi d’ eti mallon hyph’ himeron ōrse gooio,
sēmat’ anagnousēi ta hoi empeda pephrad’ Odysseus.
sentences.l:
So he spoke, and in her all the more he stirred the longing for lament,
in her who recognised the signs which Odysseus had told her, sure ones.
sentences.i: So he spoke, and all the more he stirred in her the longing to lament, as she recognised the sure signs which Odysseus had told her.
sentences.n: ὣς φάτο is the stock ‘so he spoke’, φάτο being the unaugmented imperfect. τῇ is ‘in her’, and ὑφ’ … ὦρσε is tmesis for ὑπώρσε, the aorist of ὑπόρνυμι ‘stir up’; ἵμερον γόοιο is ‘a longing for lament’. σήματ’ ἀναγνούσῃ is a dative participle, ‘her recognising the signs’, and τά οἱ ἔμπεδα πέφραδ’ Ὀδυσσεύς is ‘which Odysseus had told her, sure ones’: πέφραδε is a reduplicated aorist of φράζω ‘point out, tell’, οἱ is ‘to her’, and ἔμπεδα is ‘steadfast, sure’, neuter plural. The stranger is Odysseus, so the name stands at the end for both of them.

sentences.t: ἡ δ’ ἐπεὶ οὖν τάρφθη πολυδακρύτοιο γόοιο.
sentences.tr: hē d’ epei oun tarphthē polydakrytoio gooio.
sentences.l: And she, when she had had her fill of much-wept lament,
sentences.i: And when she had had her fill of lament and many tears,
sentences.n: This line is the same as line 213 and shows the poem’s repetition: she weeps again, as she did after the Cretan tale, and the formula returns. As printed in the source this line ends with a full stop, which looks like a misprint for a comma, since the sentence runs on into the next line; the unit follows the printing and ends here.

sentences.t: καὶ τότε μιν μύθοισιν ἀμειβομένη προσέειπε·
sentences.tr: kai tote min mythoisin ameibomenē proseeipe·
sentences.l: and then with words, answering, she addressed him:
sentences.i: and then she answered him, and spoke:
sentences.n: καὶ τότε is ‘and then’, and μύθοισιν is ‘with words’, a dative plural in -οισι of μῦθος. The rest is the reply-formula as in line 214, where ἔπεσσιν has the same meaning: the two nouns for ‘words’ are interchangeable here, and so is the English. προσέειπε is the aorist ‘addressed’.

sentences.t:
νῦν μὲν δή μοι, ξεῖνε, πάρος περ ἐὼν ἐλεεινός,
ἐν μεγάροισιν ἐμοῖσι φίλος τ’ ἔσῃ αἰδοῖός τε·
sentences.tr:
nyn men dē moi, xeine, paros per eōn eleeinos,
en megaroisin emoisi philos t’ esēi aidoios te·
sentences.l:
“Now indeed to me, stranger, though before pitiable,
in my halls you shall be both dear and honored;
sentences.i: “Now, stranger, though before you were pitiable, you shall be dear and honored in my halls;
sentences.n: Penelope’s verdict. νῦν μὲν δή μοι is ‘now indeed, to me’, and πάρος περ ἐών is ‘though being before’, with the participle in the concessive sense given by περ. ἐλεεινός is ‘pitiable’, from ἔλεος ‘pity’. ἔσῃ is the epic second person singular of the future of εἰμί, and ἐμοῖσι is a dative plural in -οισι. φίλος τ’ … αἰδοῖός τε is the welcome that a stranger gets, ‘dear and honored’, with the words in reverse order from the formula αἰδοῖός τε φίλος τε that greets a guest at arrival.

sentences.t:
αὐτὴ γὰρ τάδε εἵματ’ ἐγὼ πόρον, οἷ’ ἀγορεύεις,
πτύξασ’ ἐκ θαλάμου, περόνην τ’ ἐπέθηκα φαεινὴν
κείνῳ ἄγαλμ’ ἔμεναι·
sentences.tr:
autē gar tade heimat’ egō poron, hoi’ agoreueis,
ptyxas’ ek thalamou, peronēn t’ epethēka phaeinēn
keinōi agalm’ emenai·
sentences.i: for it was I myself who gave him these clothes you describe, taking them folded from the chamber, and I fastened a shining brooch on him as an ornament;
sentences.n: αὐτή … ἐγώ is ‘I myself’, and πόρον is the unaugmented aorist ‘gave’. οἷ’ ἀγορεύεις is ‘such as you describe’ (the relative οἷα elided). πτύξασ’ is the aorist participle of πτύσσω ‘fold’, ἐκ θαλάμου ‘out of the chamber’, and ἐπέθηκα is the aorist of ἐπιτίθημι ‘put on’; περόνην … φαεινήν is ‘a shining brooch’, with φαεινός ‘shining’. κείνῳ is ‘to that man’, and ἄγαλμ’ ἔμεναι is ‘to be an ornament’, ἔμεναι being the epic infinitive of εἰμί (Attic εἶναι). Penelope confirms the tokens, so the test is passed.

sentences.t:
τὸν δ’ οὐχ ὑποδέξομαι αὖτις
οἴκαδε νοστήσαντα φίλην ἐς πατρίδα γαῖαν.
sentences.tr:
ton d’ ouch hypodexomai autis
oikade nostēsanta philēn es patrida gaian.
sentences.l:
but him I shall not receive again
home-returned to his dear fatherland.
sentences.i: but I shall not welcome him again, come home to his dear fatherland.
sentences.n: τόν is ‘him’, and ὑποδέξομαι is the future of ὑποδέχομαι ‘receive, welcome’, with αὖτις ‘again’. οἴκαδε ‘homewards’ has the -δε suffix of direction, and νοστήσαντα is the aorist participle ‘having come home’, agreeing with τόν. φίλην ἐς πατρίδα γαῖαν is the house phrase ‘to his dear fatherland’; the stranger repeats the same words in lines 290 and 298. She has given up hope of his return.

sentences.t:
τῷ ῥα κακῇ αἴσῃ κοίλης ἐπὶ νηὸς Ὀδυσσεὺς
ᾤχετ’ ἐποψόμενος Κακοΐλιον οὐκ ὀνομαστήν.
sentences.tr:
tōi rha kakēi aisēi koilēs epi nēos Odysseus
ōichet’ epopsomenos Kakoïlion ouk onomastēn.
sentences.l:
Therefore by an evil fate on a hollow ship Odysseus
went off to look on Evil-Ilium, not to be named.”
sentences.i: That was why, by an evil fate, Odysseus went off in a hollow ship to look on Evil-Ilium, a place not to be named.”
sentences.n: τῷ ῥα is ‘therefore’, κακῇ αἴσῃ ‘by an evil fate’ (αἶσα ‘fate, portion’, a dative in -ῃ), and κοίλης ἐπὶ νηός ‘on a hollow ship’. ᾤχετ’ is the imperfect of οἴχομαι ‘go off’, and ἐποψόμενος is a future participle of purpose, ‘to look upon’. Κακοΐλιον is ‘Evil-Ilium’, a compound of κακός ‘evil’ and Ἴλιος, the name that she cannot bear to say: ὀνομαστήν is ‘to be named’, so ‘not to be named’ is ‘ill-omened, unspeakable’. The speech ends here.

sentences.t: τὴν δ’ ἀπαμειβόμενος προσέφη πολύμητις Ὀδυσσεύς·
sentences.tr: tēn d’ apameibomenos prosephē polymētis Odysseus·
sentences.l: Her answering addressed many-wiled Odysseus:
sentences.i: In answer Odysseus of many wiles said to her:
sentences.n: τὴν δ’ ἀπαμειβόμενος προσέφη πολύμητις Ὀδυσσεύς is the reply-formula again, the same line as 220: ‘answering her, many-wiled Odysseus addressed her’. It introduces the longest speech of the part, and its repetition is the point.

sentences.t:
ὦ γύναι αἰδοίη Λαερτιάδεω Ὀδυσῆος,
μηκέτι νῦν χρόα καλὸν ἐναίρεο, μηδέ τι θυμὸν
τῆκε, πόσιν γοόωσα.
sentences.tr:
ō gynai aidoiē Laertiadeō Odysēos,
mēketi nyn chroa kalon enaireo, mēde ti thymon
tēke, posin gooōsa.
sentences.l:
“O wife of Odysseus, son of Laertes, revered one,
no longer now destroy your fair skin, nor your heart at all
melt away, lamenting your husband.
sentences.i: “Revered wife of Odysseus, son of Laertes, no longer destroy your fair skin, nor melt your heart away at all in lamenting your husband.
sentences.n: ὦ γύναι αἰδοίη Λαερτιάδεω Ὀδυσῆος is ‘O wife of Odysseus, son of Laertes, revered one’: the genitives Λαερτιάδεω (in -εω) and Ὀδυσῆος (in -ῆος) depend on γύναι, the first in apposition to the second, and αἰδοίη ‘revered’ is the feminine of αἰδοῖος. μηκέτι … ἐναίρεο is a prohibition with the imperative middle of ἐναίρω ‘destroy, ruin’ (ending -εο, uncontracted); χρόα καλόν is ‘fair skin’ (χρώς), and θυμὸν τῆκε is ‘melt away your heart’ with the imperative of τήκω, taking up the image of melting from line 204. γοόωσα is ‘lamenting’.

sentences.t: νεμεσσῶμαί γε μὲν οὐδέν·
sentences.tr: nemessōmai ge men ouden·
sentences.l: I feel no indignation at all;
sentences.i: I do not blame you at all;
sentences.n: νεμεσσῶμαι is the first person of νεμεσσάομαι ‘feel righteous indignation’, contracted: so ‘I feel no indignation’, ‘I do not blame you’. γε μὲν οὐδέν is ‘not in the least’. The unit starts partway through line 264, after the full stop.

sentences.t:
καὶ γάρ τίς τ’ ἀλλοῖον ὀδύρεται ἄνδρ’ ὀλέσασα
κουρίδιον, τῷ τέκνα τέκῃ φιλότητι μιγεῖσα,
ἢ Ὀδυσῆ’, ὅν φασι θεοῖς ἐναλίγκιον εἶναι.
sentences.tr:
kai gar tis t’ alloion odyretai andr’ olesasa
kouridion, tōi tekna tekēi philotēti migeisa,
ē Odysē’, hon phasi theois enalinkion einai.
sentences.i: for even a woman who has lost a man other than Odysseus, whom they say is like the gods, mourns him, her wedded husband, to whom she bore children, joined with him in love.
sentences.n: καὶ γάρ is ‘for indeed’, and τίς τε is ‘any woman’ (the epic τε marks a general statement). ὀδύρεται is ‘laments’, and ὀλέσασα the aorist participle of ὄλλυμι, ‘having lost’. ἀλλοῖον … ἢ Ὀδυσῆ’ is ‘of another sort than Odysseus’, that is, a husband other than Odysseus; the point is that a woman weeps even for an ordinary husband, so Penelope may weep for Odysseus. κουρίδιον is ‘wedded’ (of the husband of a girl’s first marriage), and τέκῃ is an aorist subjunctive of τίκτω without ἄν in a general relative clause, ‘to whom she bears’; the English puts it in the past. μιγεῖσα is the aorist passive participle of μίγνυμι ‘mingle’, so ‘having been joined’. ἐναλίγκιος is ‘like’. θεοῖς ἐναλίγκιον εἶναι is ‘to be like the gods’.

sentences.t: ἀλλὰ γόου μὲν παῦσαι, ἐμεῖο δὲ σύνθεο μῦθον·
sentences.tr: alla goou men pausai, emeio de syntheo mython·
sentences.l: but from lament cease, and of me take in the word;
sentences.i: but leave off your lament and take my word to heart;
sentences.n: γόου … παῦσαι is ‘cease from lament’, with the aorist imperative middle of παύω and the genitive. ἐμεῖο is an old genitive ‘of me’, σύνθεο the aorist imperative middle of συντίθημι, ‘take in, lay together’, and μῦθον ‘word’ is its object.

sentences.t:
νημερτέως γάρ τοι μυθήσομαι οὐδ’ ἐπικεύσω
ὡς ἤδη Ὀδυσῆος ἐγὼ περὶ νόστου ἄκουσα
ἀγχοῦ, Θεσπρωτῶν ἀνδρῶν ἐν πίονι δήμῳ,
ζωοῦ·
sentences.tr:
nēmerteōs gar toi mythēsomai oud’ epikeusō
hōs ēdē Odysēos egō peri nostou akousa
anchou, Thesprōtōn andrōn en pioni dēmōi,
zōou·
sentences.i: for I will tell you unerringly, and I will not hide it, that I have already heard of Odysseus’s homecoming, close by, in the rich land of the Thesprotians, and that he is alive;
sentences.n: νημερτέως ‘unerringly’ is built on the adjective νημερτής, as in the house rendering ‘unerring’. μυθήσομαι is the future of μυθέομαι ‘tell’, and ἐπικεύσω the future of ἐπικεύθω ‘hide’. ὡς … ἄκουσα is ‘how, that I heard’, with the unaugmented aorist of ἀκούω and the genitive Ὀδυσῆος … νόστου ‘of Odysseus’s return’; ἀγχοῦ is ‘near’, Θεσπρωτῶν ἀνδρῶν ‘of the Thesprotian men’ (a people of north-western Greece), and ἐν πίονι δήμῳ ‘in the rich land’. ζωοῦ ‘alive’ is a genitive agreeing with Ὀδυσῆος; the unit ends at the raised dot in line 272.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἄγει κειμήλια πολλὰ καὶ ἐσθλὰ
αἰτίζων ἀνὰ δῆμον.
sentences.tr:
autar agei keimēlia polla kai esthla
aitizōn ana dēmon.
sentences.l:
but he is bringing many treasures, and good ones,
begging through the land.
sentences.i: but he is bringing many good treasures, begging his way through the land.
sentences.n: αὐτάρ ‘but’, ἄγει is ‘is bringing’, and κειμήλια are ‘treasures’, things laid up (from κεῖμαι ‘lie’). ἐσθλά is ‘good’, and αἰτίζων is ‘asking for, begging’, with ἀνὰ δῆμον ‘through the land’; the stranger makes Odysseus’s begging part of a plan to collect wealth. The unit ends at the full stop inside line 273.

sentences.t:
ἀτὰρ ἐρίηρας ἑταίρους
ὤλεσε καὶ νῆα γλαφυρὴν ἐνὶ οἴνοπι πόντῳ,
Θρινακίης ἄπο νήσου ἰών·
sentences.tr:
atar eriēras hetairous
ōlese kai nēa glaphyrēn eni oinopi pontōi,
Thrinakiēs apo nēsou iōn·
sentences.i: but his trusty companions he lost, and his hollow ship on the sea that has the look of wine, as he came away from the island of Thrinacia;
sentences.n: ἀτάρ ‘but’ is a variant of αὐτάρ. ἐρίηρας ἑταίρους is the stock phrase ‘trusty companions’, the sense of ἐρίηρος not being fully known, and ὤλεσε is the aorist of ὄλλυμι ‘lost’. νῆα γλαφυρήν is ‘a hollow ship’, and ἐνὶ οἴνοπι πόντῳ is ‘on the wine-faced open sea’ (οἶνοψ πόντος). Θρινακίης ἄπο νήσου is ‘from the island of Thrinacia’, with ἄπο standing between the adjective and its noun, and ἰών is the participle of εἶμι ‘go’. Thrinacia is where the Sun’s cattle were kept.

sentences.t:
ὀδύσαντο γὰρ αὐτῷ
Ζεύς τε καὶ Ἠέλιος·
sentences.tr:
odysanto gar autōi
Zeus te kai Ēelios·
sentences.l:
for they were angry with him,
Zeus and the Sun;
sentences.i: for Zeus and the Sun were angry with him;
sentences.n: ὀδύσαντο is the aorist middle of ὀδύσσομαι ‘be angry at’, with the dative αὐτῷ ‘with him’, and Ζεύς τε καὶ Ἠέλιος is ‘Zeus and the Sun’, Ἠέλιος being the epic form. The cause follows.

sentences.t: τοῦ γὰρ βόας ἔκταν ἑταῖροι.
sentences.tr: tou gar boas ektan hetairoi.
sentences.l: for his cattle his companions killed.
sentences.i: for his companions had killed the cattle of the Sun.
sentences.n: τοῦ is ‘his’, the Sun’s, a pronoun in the genitive; βόας is ‘cattle’ (accusative plural of βοῦς), and ἔκταν is the aorist ‘killed’ (= ἔκτειναν), with ἑταῖροι ‘companions’.

sentences.t: οἱ μὲν πάντες ὄλοντο πολυκλύστῳ ἐνὶ πόντῳ·
sentences.tr: hoi men pantes olonto polyklystōi eni pontōi·
sentences.l: They all perished in the much-washed open-sea;
sentences.i: They all perished in the wave-washed sea;
sentences.n: οἱ is ‘they’, and ὄλοντο is the unaugmented aorist middle of ὄλλυμι, ‘perished’. πολυκλύστῳ is ‘much-washed’, from κλύζω ‘wash, dash’, so ‘heavily beaten by waves’, a dative in -ῳ agreeing with πόντῳ.

sentences.t:
τὸν δ’ ἄρ’ ἐπὶ τρόπιος νεὸς ἔκβαλε κῦμ’ ἐπὶ χέρσου,
Φαιήκων ἐς γαῖαν, οἳ ἀγχίθεοι γεγάασιν,
sentences.tr:
ton d’ ar’ epi tropios neos ekbale kym’ epi chersou,
Phaiēkōn es gaian, hoi anchitheoi gegaasin,
sentences.l:
but him, on the keel of his ship, a wave cast out on the dry land,
to the land of the Phaeacians, who are close to the gods,
sentences.i: but him, on the keel of his ship, a wave cast out on the dry land, in the land of the Phaeacians, who are close to the gods,
sentences.n: τόν is ‘him’, and ἐπὶ τρόπιος νεός is ‘on the keel of the ship’ (νεός is νηός). ἔκβαλε is the aorist of ἐκβάλλω ‘cast out’, κῦμ’ the subject ‘a wave’, and ἐπὶ χέρσου is ‘onto dry land’. Φαιήκων ἐς γαῖαν is ‘to the land of the Phaeacians’, and οἳ ἀγχίθεοι γεγάασιν is ‘who are close to the gods’, ἀγχίθεος being ἀγχι- ‘near’ with θεός and γεγάασιν the epic perfect of γίγνομαι (= γεγόνασι). The unit stops at the comma, since the clause would otherwise run past four lines.

sentences.t:
οἳ δή μιν περὶ κῆρι θεὸν ὣς τιμήσαντο
καί οἱ πολλὰ δόσαν πέμπειν τέ μιν ἤθελον αὐτοὶ
οἴκαδ’ ἀπήμαντον.
sentences.tr:
hoi dē min peri kēri theon hōs timēsanto
kai hoi polla dosan pempein te min ēthelon autoi
oikad’ apēmanton.
sentences.l:
who indeed honored him in their hearts as a god
and gave him many things, and were willing to send him themselves
home unharmed.
sentences.i: who honored him in their hearts like a god, and gave him many things, and were themselves willing to send him home unharmed.
sentences.n: οἳ δή is ‘who indeed’. τιμήσαντο is the aorist middle of τιμάω ‘honor’, with θεὸν ὥς ‘as a god’ and περὶ κῆρι ‘in the heart’ (κῆρι is an old locative of κῆρ). δόσαν is the unaugmented aorist ‘gave’, and πέμπειν … ἤθελον is ‘were willing to send’, with αὐτοί ‘themselves’. οἴκαδ’ ἀπήμαντον is ‘home unharmed’, ἀπήμαντος having a privative ἀ- and the root of πῆμα ‘harm’. The unit ends at the full stop inside line 282.

sentences.t:
καί κεν πάλαι ἐνθάδ’ Ὀδυσσεὺς
ἤην·
sentences.tr:
kai ken palai enthad’ Odysseus
ēēn·
sentences.l:
And long ago here Odysseus
would have been;
sentences.i: And Odysseus would long ago have been here;
sentences.n: καί κεν πάλαι is ‘and long ago … would’, with κεν the epic ἄν; ἤην is the epic imperfect ‘was’ (ἦν), so the combination means ‘would have been here’. The raised dot ends the unit in mid-line, and the objection follows.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ἄρα οἱ τό γε κέρδιον εἴσατο θυμῷ,
χρήματ’ ἀγυρτάζειν πολλὴν ἐπὶ γαῖαν ἰόντι·
sentences.tr:
all’ ara hoi to ge kerdion eisato thymōi,
chrēmat’ agyrtazein pollēn epi gaian ionti·
sentences.l:
but this seemed better to him in his heart,
to gather goods, going over much country;
sentences.i: but it seemed better to him in his heart to gather goods as he went over much country;
sentences.n: ἀλλ’ ἄρα is ‘but then’, and οἱ is ‘to him’. τό γε κέρδιον is ‘this the better thing’ (κέρδιον ‘better, more profitable’), and εἴσατο is the aorist middle of εἴδομαι ‘seemed’, with θυμῷ ‘in his heart’. ἀγυρτάζειν is ‘to collect’, as a beggar or collector does, and χρήματ’ is ‘goods’. πολλὴν ἐπὶ γαῖαν ἰόντι is ‘to him going over much country’, a dative participle agreeing with οἱ.

sentences.t:
ὣς περὶ κέρδεα πολλὰ καταθνητῶν ἀνθρώπων
οἶδ’ Ὀδυσεύς, οὐδ’ ἄν τις ἐρίσσειε βροτὸς ἄλλος.
sentences.tr:
hōs peri kerdea polla katathnētōn anthrōpōn
oid’ Odyseus, oud’ an tis erisseie brotos allos.
sentences.l:
so beyond mortal men many cunning-ways
Odysseus knows, nor could any other mortal rival him.
sentences.i: So many cunning ways does Odysseus know beyond mortal men, and no other mortal could rival him.
sentences.n: ὣς περί is ‘so greatly beyond’, with the genitive καταθνητῶν ἀνθρώπων ‘mortal men’ (καταθνητός ‘subject to death’). κέρδεα … οἶδ’ is ‘knows cunning-ways’, the house rendering of the phrase for Odysseus’s craft, where κέρδεα are ‘gains, profitable tricks’. ἐρίσσειε is an optative in a potential clause with ἄν, ‘could contend with’, and βροτὸς ἄλλος ‘any other mortal’.

sentences.t: ὥς μοι Θεσπρωτῶν βασιλεὺς μυθήσατο Φείδων·
sentences.tr: hōs moi Thesprōtōn basileus mythēsato Pheidōn·
sentences.l: So to me the king of the Thesprotians told, Pheidon;
sentences.i: So Pheidon, the king of the Thesprotians, told me;
sentences.n: ὥς is ‘so’ (with an accent, as the adverb), and μυθήσατο is the aorist of μυθέομαι ‘tell’. Θεσπρωτῶν βασιλεύς is ‘king of the Thesprotians’, and Φείδων is the name Pheidon, placed last in the line.

sentences.t:
ὤμνυε δὲ πρὸς ἔμ’ αὐτόν, ἀποσπένδων ἐνὶ οἴκῳ,
νῆα κατειρύσθαι καὶ ἐπαρτέας ἔμμεν ἑταίρους,
οἳ δή μιν πέμψουσι φίλην ἐς πατρίδα γαῖαν.
sentences.tr:
ōmnye de pros em’ auton, apospendōn eni oikōi,
nēa kateirysthai kai eparteas emmen hetairous,
hoi dē min pempsousi philēn es patrida gaian.
sentences.l:
And he was swearing, to me myself, pouring a libation in his house,
that a ship had been drawn down and that ready were companions
who indeed would send him to his dear fatherland.
sentences.i: And in his house, pouring a libation, he swore to me in person that a ship had been drawn down and that companions were ready who were to send Odysseus on to his dear fatherland.
sentences.n: ὤμνυε is the imperfect of ὄμνυμι ‘swear’, ‘was swearing’, and πρὸς ἔμ’ αὐτόν is ‘to me myself’, ἀποσπένδων ‘pouring a libation’. κατειρύσθαι is the perfect passive infinitive of κατερύω ‘draw down’ (a launched ship), and ἔμμεν is ἔμμεναι ‘be’ with ἐπαρτέας ‘ready’. οἳ δή μιν πέμψουσι is a relative clause in the future, ‘who were to send him’, and φίλην ἐς πατρίδα γαῖαν is ‘to his dear fatherland’.

sentences.t: ἀλλ’ ἐμὲ πρὶν ἀπέπεμψε·
sentences.tr: all’ eme prin apepempse·
sentences.l: But me before that he sent away;
sentences.i: But he sent me away before that;
sentences.n: ἀλλ’ ἐμὲ πρίν is ‘but me before’ (before the ship), and ἀπέπεμψε is the aorist ‘sent off’. The unit ends at the raised dot inside line 291.

sentences.t:
τύχησε γὰρ ἐρχομένη νηῦς
ἀνδρῶν Θεσπρωτῶν ἐς Δουλίχιον πολύπυρον.
sentences.tr:
tychēse gar erchomenē nēus
andrōn Thesprōtōn es Doulichion polypyron.
sentences.l:
for happened going a ship
of Thesprotian men to Dulichium, rich in wheat.
sentences.i: for a ship of Thesprotian men happened to be on its way to Dulichium, rich in wheat.
sentences.n: τύχησε is the aorist of τυγχάνω ‘happen’, with the participle ἐρχομένη ‘going’ agreeing with νηῦς ‘ship’; the construction is ‘a ship happened going’, that is, ‘happened to be on its way’. ἀνδρῶν Θεσπρωτῶν is ‘of Thesprotian men’, and ἐς Δουλίχιον πολύπυρον is ‘to Dulichium, rich in wheat’ (πολύπυρος, from πυρός ‘wheat’), an island whose place is not certain.

sentences.t: καί μοι κτήματ’ ἔδειξεν, ὅσα ξυναγείρατ’ Ὀδυσσεύς·
sentences.tr: kai moi ktēmat’ edeixen, hosa xynageirat’ Odysseus·
sentences.l: and to me goods he showed, as many as Odysseus had gathered together;
sentences.i: and he showed me the goods, as many as Odysseus had gathered together;
sentences.n: κτήματ’ is ‘goods’ (the neuter plural of κτῆμα, with elision), and ἔδειξεν is the aorist of δείκνυμι ‘show’. ὅσα ξυναγείρατ’ is ‘as many as he had gathered together’, with the aorist middle of συναγείρω in the epic form ξυν-. The stranger keeps naming proofs that can be checked.

sentences.t:
καί νύ κεν ἐς δεκάτην γενεὴν ἕτερόν γ’ ἔτι βόσκοι,
ὅσσα οἱ ἐν μεγάροις κειμήλια κεῖτο ἄνακτος.
sentences.tr:
kai ny ken es dekatēn geneēn heteron g’ eti boskoi,
hossa hoi en megarois keimēlia keito anaktos.
sentences.l:
and indeed to the tenth generation another still it might feed,
so many treasures lay for him in the halls of the lord.
sentences.i: and it could still feed another man, even to the tenth generation, so many treasures lay for him in the halls of the lord.
sentences.n: καί νυ κεν is ‘and indeed … would’ (νύ is the particle ‘now’), and ἐς δεκάτην γενεήν is ‘to the tenth generation’. βόσκοι is an optative of βόσκω ‘feed’, so ‘could feed’, with ἕτερόν γ’ ἔτι ‘another still’. ὅσσα … κειμήλια κεῖτο is ‘so many treasures lay’: κεῖτο is the unaugmented imperfect of κεῖμαι ‘lie’, with a neuter plural subject and a singular verb; οἱ is ‘for him’, and ἄνακτος ‘of the lord’ is Pheidon, whose halls kept Odysseus’s goods. The unit passes over the comma at the end of line 294, since it is the middle of a clause.

sentences.t:
τὸν δ’ ἐς Δωδώνην φάτο βήμεναι, ὄφρα θεοῖο
ἐκ δρυὸς ὑψικόμοιο Διὸς βουλὴν ἐπακούσαι,
ὅππως νοστήσειε φίλην ἐς πατρίδα γαῖαν
ἤδη δὴν ἀπεών, ἢ ἀμφαδὸν ἦε κρυφηδόν.
sentences.tr:
ton d’ es Dōdōnēn phato bēmenai, ophra theoio
ek dryos hypsikomoio Dios boulēn epakousai,
hoppōs nostēseie philēn es patrida gaian
ēdē dēn apeōn, ē amphadon ēe kryphēdon.
sentences.l:
And him to Dodona he said had gone, in order that of the god
from the high-crowned oak the plan of Zeus he might hear,
how he might return to his dear fatherland
already long away, whether openly or in secret.
sentences.i: He said that Odysseus had gone to Dodona, to hear the plan of Zeus from the high-crowned oak of the god, how he might return to his dear fatherland, after being long away already, whether openly or in secret.
sentences.n: τόν is ‘him’, Odysseus, and φάτο βήμεναι is ‘said he had gone’: φάτο is the unaugmented imperfect ‘said’, and βήμεναι the epic infinitive of βαίνω ‘go’. Δωδώνη is Dodona, the oracle of Zeus, with the god’s plan heard ἐκ δρυὸς ὑψικόμοιο ‘from the high-crowned oak’ (ὑψίκομος, ‘high-crowned’, from κόμη ‘hair, foliage’); ὄφρα … ἐπακούσαι is a purpose clause with the aorist optative. ὅππως νοστήσειε is an indirect question, ‘how he might come home’, and φίλην ἐς πατρίδα γαῖαν is ‘to his dear fatherland’. ἀπεών ‘being away’ is the Ionic participle of ἄπειμι, and ἀμφαδόν and κρυφηδόν are ‘openly’ and ‘secretly’.

sentences.t:
ὣς ὁ μὲν οὕτως ἐστὶ σόος καὶ ἐλεύσεται ἤδη
ἄγχι μάλ’, οὐδ’ ἔτι τῆλε φίλων καὶ πατρίδος αἴης
δηρὸν ἀπεσσεῖται·
sentences.tr:
hōs ho men houtōs esti soos kai eleusetai ēdē
anchi mal’, oud’ eti tēle philōn kai patridos aiēs
dēron apesseitai·
sentences.i: So he is safe, and will come now, very near; no longer will he be far from his dear ones and his fatherland for long;
sentences.n: ὣς ὁ μὲν οὕτως ἐστί is ‘so he thus is’, with σόος ‘safe’ (the uncontracted form of σῶς). ἐλεύσεται is the future of ἔρχομαι ‘come’, ἤδη ‘now’, and ἄγχι μάλ’ ‘very near’. οὐδ’ ἔτι τῆλε is ‘nor any longer far’, with the genitives φίλων καὶ πατρίδος αἴης ‘from his dear ones and his fatherland’ (αἶα is the poetic word for land; πατρὶς αἶα is a variant of πατρὶς γαῖα). δηρὸν ἀπεσσεῖται is ‘will be away for long’, the epic future of ἄπειμι. The unit ends at the raised dot inside line 302.

sentences.t: ἔμπης δέ τοι ὅρκια δώσω.
sentences.tr: empēs de toi horkia dōsō.
sentences.l: but still, to you a pledge I will give.
sentences.i: Even so, I will give you a sworn pledge.
sentences.n: ἔμπης is ‘all the same, even so’, and τοι is ‘to you’; ὅρκια is the neuter plural ‘sworn pledges, an oath’, and δώσω the future of δίδωμι ‘give’. He offers an oath, not proof, since proof cannot be shown yet.

sentences.t:
ἴστω νῦν Ζεὺς πρῶτα, θεῶν ὕπατος καὶ ἄριστος,
ἱστίη τ’ Ὀδυσῆος ἀμύμονος, ἣν ἀφικάνω·
sentences.tr:
istō nyn Zeus prōta, theōn hypatos kai aristos,
histiē t’ Odysēos amymonos, hēn aphikanō·
sentences.l:
Let Zeus now know first, highest and best of the gods,
and the hearth of blameless Odysseus, to which I have come;
sentences.i: Let Zeus now know first, highest and best of the gods, and the hearth of blameless Odysseus, to which I have come;
sentences.n: ἴστω is the third-person imperative of οἶδα ‘know’; to call a power to ‘know’ is to call it to witness. Ζεύς is named first (πρῶτα), with θεῶν ὕπατος καὶ ἄριστος ‘highest and best of the gods’ (ὕπατος is ‘highest’). ἱστίη is the Ionic form of Attic ἑστία ‘hearth’, ἀμύμονος is ‘blameless’ by the house rendering, though the real meaning of ἀμύμων is not known, and ἥν ἀφικάνω is ‘to which I have come’, ἀφικάνω being a lengthened present of ἀφικνέομαι. The hearth is the one that welcomes a guest.

sentences.t: ἦ μέν τοι τάδε πάντα τελείεται ὡς ἀγορεύω.
sentences.tr: ē men toi tade panta teleietai hōs agoreuō.
sentences.l: Truly to you all these things will be fulfilled, as I say.
sentences.i: All this will truly come about, just as I say.
sentences.n: ἦ μέν is ‘truly’, and τοι is ‘to you’; τελείεται is the epic present of τελέω ‘fulfil’, here with a future sense, ‘will be fulfilled’. ὡς ἀγορεύω is ‘as I say’, ἀγορεύω being the verb ‘speak’. The line ends the oath and sets up the date.

sentences.t:
τοῦδ’ αὐτοῦ λυκάβαντος ἐλεύσεται ἐνθάδ’ Ὀδυσσεύς,
τοῦ μὲν φθίνοντος μηνός, τοῦ δ’ ἱσταμένοιο.
sentences.tr:
toud’ autou lykabantos eleusetai enthad’ Odysseus,
tou men phthinontos mēnos, tou d’ histamenoio.
sentences.l:
Within this very year will come here Odysseus,
as the one month wanes and the other begins.”
sentences.i: Within this very year Odysseus will come here, at the turn of the month, as one wanes and the next begins.”
sentences.n: τοῦδ’ αὐτοῦ is ‘this very’, and λυκάβαντος is the genitive of λυκάβας, ‘year’ by tradition, though the word’s exact sense is not certain. ἐλεύσεται ἐνθάδ’ is ‘will come here’, with the genitive of time in the phrase. τοῦ μὲν φθίνοντος μηνός, τοῦ δ’ ἱσταμένοιο is ‘of the one month waning, the other beginning’, a pair of genitive absolutes in which τοῦ is the pronoun: the date is the turn of the month. The unit closes the speech.
